questions.q: What makes an object a transformer rather than just an estimator?
options: It must be a classification model
It has a transform method that returns a changed version of the data
It never needs to be fitted
It always outputs a single number
questions.explain: A transformer is an estimator (it learns with fit) that also offers transform, which applies what was learned to produce a modified table.

questions.q: You have a fitted StandardScaler called scaler. How should you prepare the test set?
options: scaler.fit_transform(X_test), so it is centered on its own mean
Fit a second scaler on the test set
scaler.transform(X_test), reusing the mean and spread learned from training
Leave the test set unscaled
questions.explain: The scaler's numbers must come from training data only. Calling transform on the test set applies them without letting test rows influence the preprocessing.

options: StandardScaler
SimpleImputer
OneHotEncoder
RandomForestClassifier
questions.explain: Predictors have predict and turn features into answers. Scalers, imputers, and encoders are transformers.

options: A new, unfitted estimator with the same settings
The same fitted object under a new name
A copy including all learned coefficients
A list of the estimator's hyperparameters
questions.explain: clone copies the constructor settings but none of the learned state, which is why cross-validation and search tools can use it to start each run cleanly.

questions.q: After imputer.fit(X_train), where does the learned median for each column live?
options: In imputer.median
In imputer.statistics_, an attribute ending in an underscore
In X_train itself
Nowhere; it is recomputed on every transform
questions.explain: SimpleImputer stores its per-column fill values in statistics_. The trailing underscore marks values learned during fit.
